title: Maximum Array Hopping Score II
statement: You start at index `0` of the integer array `nums` and must finish exactly at its last index. Each hop moves you from your current index `i` to any index `j` with `j > i` and earns `(j - i) * nums[j]` points. Return the largest total score that a sequence of hops from index `0` to the last index can earn.
notes:
## Intuition

Picture the trip from index 0 to the last index as `n - 1` unit steps. A hop from `i` to `j` covers the steps that end at `i + 1`, ..., `j`, and pays `nums[j]` for each of them. So the step that ends at index `k` is paid by the value where its hop lands, an index at or after `k`, which is at most the largest value in `nums[k..]`. Always hopping to the largest value ahead meets that bound for every step at once, so it is optimal. A DP over every landing point (the brute force) also works but costs O(n²).

## Approach

1. Scan from the right to fill `next[i]`, the index of the largest value in `nums[i..n - 1]`. On ties keep the farther index: it saves hops without changing the score.
2. Start at `position = 0` with `score = 0`.
3. Until `position` is the last index, hop to `target = next[position + 1]`, the largest value strictly ahead, and add `(target - position) * nums[target]`.
4. Return `score`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 5, 8]`. The scan gives `next = [2, 2, 2]`. From `position = 0`, the largest value ahead is `8` at index 2, so a single hop earns `(2 - 0) * 8 = 16` and reaches the end. The two short hops 0 → 1 → 2 would earn only `5 + 8 = 13`. The answer is 16. (In Example 2 the hops are 0 → 4 onto the 9 and 4 → 6 onto the 3: `4 * 9 + 2 * 3 = 42`.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one scan to fill `next` and at most `n - 1` hops.
- Space: O(n) for `next`; a running maximum taken from the right could add up the same per-step values in O(1) space.

## Pitfalls

- Hopping one index at a time, or to the nearest bigger value, is not optimal: Example 1's single long hop beats both.
- Look strictly ahead with `next[position + 1]`: `next[position]` can be `position` itself, and the loop would never move.
- With LeetCode's limits the score can reach about 10^10, beyond 32 bits: Java and C need a `long` total.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `next` | `next[i]`: index of the largest value in `nums[i..n - 1]` |
| `i` | index being filled during the right-to-left scan |
| `position` | index where the current hop starts |
| `target` | index the greedy hop lands on |
| `score` | total score of the hops so far |

narration.2: n is the number of values; the trip must end at index n - 1.
narration.3: next[i] will hold the index of the largest value from i to the end; the last index starts as its own answer.
narration.4: Fill next from right to left so each entry can reuse the one after it.
narration.5: Index i wins only if its value beats the best value after it; ties keep the farther index.
narration.7: No hops yet, so the score is 0.
narration.9: Keep hopping until the last index is reached.
narration.10: Greedy choice: land on the largest value strictly ahead of position.
narration.11: Each of the target - position unit steps of this hop is paid nums[target].
narration.14: Return the total score of the greedy hops.
